flags: minor: wrong choice A (Congress) is flatly contradicted in P4 and C (trains ran late) is unsupported, so B wins quickly; distractor D duplicates the idea of R037-09 choice C
R037-01.notes: P5 thesis: noon moved from a fact about the sky to an agreement; railroads, not Congress, did it. B paraphrases this. A and D are contradicted by P4; C invents a cause.

R037-02.notes: P1: the sun moves westward, so Boston noon comes before New York and Chicago noon comes after both. A town farther west reaches noon later still. This takes one extension step, and students who mix up the direction may pick A.

R037-03.notes: Each clock is correct for some line and none for the street, so the image illustrates the confusion of each railroad keeping its own time. C is the opposite; B and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: 'set places at set times' is a light inference from 'had to meet and pass at sidings'. The other choices are unsupported, so this is close to a lookup
R037-04.notes: P2: opposing trains had to meet and pass at sidings, and that only works if both crews agree on the time.

flags: minor: the key closely paraphrases the P3 sentence ('where local noon had already passed, clocks were turned back ... noon arrived a second time'), so the item is a lookup
minor: 'set back to noon' is slightly stronger than the passage's 'turned back several minutes', but it is defensible
R037-05.notes: Towns east of the meridian were already past local noon; their clocks went back several minutes, so they hit noon again. B has the wrong direction; C and D are invented.

flags: minor: D is awkwardly worded ('granting their legal point but not that it explained the change'), is not parallel with the 'adjective, because...' form of A-C, and is the only nuanced choice, which cues it
minor: B ('fully supportive') and C ('indifferent') are weak distractors
R037-06.notes: 'They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority at all. They had something more effective...' The author concedes the legal point but holds that the railroads' power came from the network. A is a possible trap because the author does undercut the objectors, but he does not say they misunderstood the law.

R037-07.notes: 'What is striking is who made the change' means it is noteworthy or remarkable. 'Forceful' is the main literal-meaning trap.

flags: minor: strictly, clocks running before solar noon also happened under local mean time because of the equation of time. P1 also defines local noon as the sun's highest point while P3 speaks of 'mean time', a small simplification. Neither point affects the key
R037-08.notes: Under standard time, noon is set by agreement, not by the sun. Only B shows clock noon cut loose from the sun's position. A and D show the old sky-based meaning; C shows pre-1883 railroad confusion, a plausible trap for students who link 'disagreeing clocks' to convention.

flags: minor: choice C ('most American cities refused ... until 1918') repeats the idea of R037-01 choice D; both are contradicted by 'Many cities adjusted their own clocks within weeks'
R037-09.notes: P4 says the railroads announced a schedule and the public followed with no law required. The 1918 date shows that practice came before law (35 years). B and D are unsupported; C is contradicted.
